decks.title: Retirement and Death of a Partner — Part 1: Ratios, Goodwill, Revaluation and Reserves
goals: Calculate the new ratio and the gaining ratio when a partner retires or dies, including a continuing partner who sacrifices
Adjust the outgoing partner's share of goodwill (stated or hidden) through the gaining partners under Accounting Standard 26, and write off book goodwill
Prepare the Revaluation Account and distribute reserves and accumulated losses among all the partners

slides.heading: Reconstitution: Retirement and Death of a Partner
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **ratios**, **goodwill**, **revaluation** and **reserves** when a partner leaves. Every firm, person and figure in this chapter is imagined.

nodes.label: Retirement and death
New and gaining ratios
Goodwill, including hidden goodwill
Revaluation Account
Reserves and accumulated losses

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: retirement and death, the new and gaining ratios, goodwill including hidden goodwill, the revaluation account, and reserves and accumulated losses
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: When a partner retires or dies, the old agreement ends, but the business usually carries on with the partners who remain. The books are reconstituted, not closed. Before the outgoing partner is paid, we must work out the new ratio and the gaining ratio, settle goodwill, revalue the assets and liabilities, and share out the reserves. That is this first part.

slides.heading: Retirement and death under the Act
bullets: A partner **retires** with the consent of all the others, under an express agreement, or by notice when the partnership is at will.
Unless the deed says otherwise, **death** dissolves the firm; most deeds let the survivors carry on.

rows: With the consent of all other partners, under an express agreement, or by notice in a partnership at will (Section 32)
Dissolves the firm unless the deed provides that the others carry on (Section 42)
Usually at the end of an accounting year
Any day of the year: profit till death must be worked out

visual.alt: Table comparing retirement and death of a partner: how each happens under the Indian Partnership Act, when it usually happens, who is paid, and where the unpaid balance is carried
visual.caption: Indian Partnership Act, 1932.

slides.narration: Under the Indian Partnership Act, a partner may retire with everyone else's consent, under an express agreement, or by notice when the partnership is at will. Death, unless the deed says otherwise, dissolves the firm, so most deeds let the others continue. Retirement usually happens at the year end, but death can come on any day, so we also work out profit up to the date of death.

slides.heading: What must be settled
slides.body_md: The outgoing partner is entitled to his capital **plus** his share of everything the firm earned or built up while he was a partner.

nodes.label: New ratio and gaining ratio
Goodwill
Revaluation Account
Reserves and accumulated profits or losses
Profit till death (on death)
Amount due: paid, loan or executor
Capitals and the new Balance Sheet

visual.alt: Flow of the matters settled when a partner retires or dies: the new and gaining ratios, goodwill, revaluation, reserves and accumulated profits or losses, profit till death on death, the amount due paid or carried as a loan, and capitals with the new balance sheet
visual.caption: What is settled when a partner leaves

slides.narration: Seven matters are settled in order. First the new ratio and the gaining ratio. Then goodwill, revaluation, and reserves or accumulated losses. On death, profit up to the date of death is added. Then the amount due is paid, or kept as a loan. Finally the continuing partners may adjust their capitals and a new balance sheet is drawn up.

slides.heading: New ratio and gaining ratio

headers: Terms on which the outgoing share is taken
New share of a continuing partner
rows: In the old ratio of the continuing partners
A stated fraction **of the firm** is acquired
The outgoing share is taken in a given ratio
Old share + outgoing share × his part of that ratio

visual.alt: Table of the ways the outgoing partner's share is taken: with nothing agreed the continuing partners keep their old ratio; a fraction of the firm acquired is added to the old share; a share taken in a given ratio is split in that ratio; with a stated new ratio, gain is new minus old and may be negative
visual.caption: In every case: gain = new share − old share.

slides.narration: The outgoing share always passes to the partners who stay, but the terms differ. If nothing is agreed, they carry on in their old ratio. They may acquire stated fractions of the firm, or take the outgoing share in a given ratio, or simply state a new ratio. In every case, gain equals new share minus old share, and with a stated ratio a partner may even lose.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: nothing agreed
slides.body_md: Gulmohar Marble Polishers, Kishangarh (imagined): Anshuman, Bhairavi and Chiranjeev share **3 : 2 : 1**. Bhairavi retires on 31 March 2026 and nothing is agreed about future shares.

visual.alt: Table of worked example one: Anshuman rises from six twelfths to nine twelfths and Chiranjeev from two twelfths to three twelfths; Bhairavi's four twelfths is shared three to one; the new ratio and the gaining ratio are both three to one
visual.caption: Nothing agreed: the continuing partners keep their old ratio.

slides.narration: With nothing agreed, Anshuman and Chiranjeev keep their old ratio of three to one. Anshuman's share rises from one half to three quarters, a gain of one quarter. Chiranjeev's rises from one sixth to one quarter, a gain of one twelfth. So the gaining ratio is also three to one.

visual.caption: Shares before and after Bhairavi retires (worked example 1).

slides.narration: Each bar is the whole profit of the firm. Before, Bhairavi holds one third. After she retires, her third is shared by Anshuman and Chiranjeev in the ratio three to one, so Anshuman grows to three quarters and Chiranjeev to one quarter. Both bars are the same length, because the shares always add up to one.

slides.heading: Quick check: fractions acquired
slides.body_md: Add what each partner acquires to his old share.
slides.narration: Each continuing partner acquires a stated fraction of the whole profit. Add it straight to his old share.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a stated new ratio
slides.body_md: Kesar Coir Mats, Karunagappally (imagined): Devyani, Edwin and Gajendra share **2 : 2 : 1**. Devyani retires; Edwin and Gajendra agree to share **equally**.

visual.alt: Table of worked example two: Edwin rises from four tenths to five tenths, a gain of one tenth; Gajendra rises from two tenths to five tenths, a gain of three tenths; the gaining ratio is one to three, not their old ratio of two to one
visual.caption: Devyani's 4/10 = Edwin's 1/10 + Gajendra's 3/10.

slides.narration: Write the shares in tenths. Edwin moves from four tenths to five tenths, a gain of one tenth. Gajendra moves from two tenths to five tenths, a gain of three tenths. The gaining ratio is one to three. It is neither the old ratio of two to one nor the new ratio of one to one, so it must always be worked out.

slides.heading: Sacrificing ratio and gaining ratio

rows: Retirement or death (or a change in ratio)
Credit the newcomer's premium to those who give up profit
Charge the outgoing partner's goodwill to those who gain

visual.alt: Table contrasting the sacrificing ratio, which arises on admission and is old share minus new share, with the gaining ratio, which arises on retirement or death and is new share minus old share

slides.narration: The two ratios are mirror images. The sacrificing ratio arises when a partner joins: it is old share minus new share, and it shares out the premium he brings. The gaining ratio arises when a partner leaves: it is new share minus old share, and it shows who pays the outgoing partner for goodwill.

slides.heading: Goodwill on retirement or death
bullets: Outgoing partner's share = firm's goodwill × his share, credited to him.
Debited to the **gaining partners** in the **gaining ratio**; no goodwill account is raised.

nodes.label: Outgoing partner built part of the reputation
Continuing partners will enjoy his share of future profits
Gaining partners debited, outgoing partner credited
No goodwill account (Accounting Standard 26)

visual.alt: Flow: the outgoing partner built part of the firm's reputation; the continuing partners will enjoy his share of future profits; so the gaining partners are debited and he is credited; no goodwill account is raised under Accounting Standard 26
visual.caption: Why the gaining partners pay

slides.narration: The outgoing partner helped build the firm's reputation, but the future profits it brings will go to those who stay. So the partners who gain his share pay him for it. His share equals the firm's goodwill times his profit share, and it is debited to the gaining partners in their gaining ratio. Accounting Standard twenty-six does not allow a goodwill account to be opened.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a continuing partner who sacrifices
slides.body_md: Mogra Kite Makers, Badlapur (imagined): Hiranmayi, Jaiveer and Kaustubh share **5 : 3 : 2**. Kaustubh retires; Hiranmayi and Jaiveer agree on **2 : 3**. Goodwill is ₹1,50,000.

rows: *(Being Kaustubh's share of goodwill and Hiranmayi's sacrifice charged to Jaiveer, who gains 3/10)*

visual.alt: Journal of worked example three: Jaiveer's capital debited 45,000 rupees, crediting Kaustubh's capital 30,000 and Hiranmayi's capital 15,000, because Hiranmayi also gives up a tenth

slides.narration: Hiranmayi falls from five tenths to four tenths, so she sacrifices one tenth even though a partner is leaving. Jaiveer rises from three tenths to six tenths, a gain of three tenths. Jaiveer alone pays: rupees forty-five thousand. Kaustubh receives two tenths of the goodwill, rupees thirty thousand, and Hiranmayi receives one tenth, rupees fifteen thousand.

slides.heading: Book goodwill and hidden goodwill
bullets: Goodwill already in the books is written off among **all** partners, old ratio.
If the outgoing partner is paid **more** than his adjusted capital, the excess is his share of **hidden goodwill**.

nodes.label: Goodwill already in the books: write off among ALL partners, old ratio
Agreed settlement − his capital after all other adjustments = his share of hidden goodwill
His share ÷ his profit share = goodwill of the firm
Gaining partners debited, outgoing partner credited

visual.alt: Flow for goodwill already in the books and hidden goodwill: book goodwill is written off among all the partners in the old ratio; the excess of the agreed settlement over the outgoing capital is his share of hidden goodwill; dividing by his share gives the firm's goodwill; the gaining partners are debited
visual.caption: Book goodwill and hidden goodwill

slides.narration: Goodwill already shown in the books is first written off among all the partners in the old ratio. Sometimes nothing is said about goodwill, but the others agree to pay the outgoing partner a lump sum. If that sum is more than his capital after all other adjustments, the excess is his share of hidden goodwill. Divide it by his profit share to value the firm's goodwill.

slides.heading: Quick check: paying more than the capital
slides.body_md: Where does the excess go?
slides.narration: Think about who is paying the excess and who is receiving it.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: hidden goodwill
slides.body_md: Taragarh Pickle House, Beawar (imagined): Mayank, Nivedita and Omesh share **2 : 2 : 1**. Omesh retires; his capital after all other adjustments is ₹74,000, and he is to be paid ₹92,000 in full settlement.

rows: Omesh's capital after all other adjustments

visual.alt: Table of worked example four: Omesh is paid 92,000 against a capital of 74,000, so his share of hidden goodwill is 18,000 and the firm's goodwill 90,000; Mayank and Nivedita are charged 9,000 each
visual.caption: Entry: Mayank's and Nivedita's Capital A/cs Dr. ₹9,000 each To Omesh's Capital A/c ₹18,000.

slides.narration: Omesh will receive rupees ninety-two thousand, but his capital is only rupees seventy-four thousand. The difference, rupees eighteen thousand, is his share of hidden goodwill. His share is one fifth, so the firm's goodwill is rupees ninety thousand. Mayank and Nivedita gain equally and are charged rupees nine thousand each.

slides.heading: Quick check: hidden goodwill
slides.body_md: Settlement minus adjusted capital, then divide by his share.
slides.narration: Find his share of goodwill first, then scale it up to the whole firm. Give your answer in rupees.

slides.heading: The Revaluation Account on retirement or death
slides.body_md: Same format as on admission, but the result is shared by **all** the partners, the outgoing one included.

rows: Fall in the value of an asset
Rise in the value of an asset
Rise in a liability; unrecorded liability
Fall in a liability; unrecorded asset

visual.alt: Table of the revaluation account on retirement: losses on the debit side, gains on the credit side, and the balance shared by all the partners, the outgoing one included, in the old ratio
visual.caption: Also called the Profit and Loss Adjustment Account.

slides.narration: The revaluation account works as it did on admission. Losses go on the debit side and gains on the credit side. The difference is that the outgoing partner was a member while those values changed, so the profit or loss is shared by all the partners, him included, in the old ratio.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: the starting balance sheet
slides.body_md: Gulmohar Marble Polishers again. On Bhairavi's retirement: premises up 15%, machinery down 10%, a 5% provision on debtors, and an unrecorded rent bill.

visual.alt: Balance sheet of Gulmohar Marble Polishers before Bhairavi retires, totalling 4,98,000 rupees: creditors, general reserve, workmen compensation reserve and three capitals; bank, debtors, stock, machinery, premises, furniture and advertisement suspense
visual.caption: Balance Sheet as at 31 March 2026 (horizontal form).

slides.narration: Here is the balance sheet of Gulmohar Marble Polishers on the day Bhairavi retires, in horizontal form. Look out for three items that will be shared among all three partners: the general reserve of rupees thirty-six thousand, the workmen compensation reserve, and the advertisement suspense on the assets side.

slides.heading: Worked example 5 (continued): Revaluation Account
slides.body_md: Premises up ₹27,000; machinery down ₹11,000; provision ₹3,000; outstanding rent ₹1,000.

rows: To Provision for Doubtful Debts A/c

visual.alt: Revaluation account of Gulmohar Marble Polishers: machinery 11,000, provision 3,000 and outstanding rent 1,000 on the debit side; premises 27,000 on the credit side; profit 12,000 rupees shared three to two to one

slides.narration: The losses are machinery eleven thousand, the provision three thousand and the rent bill one thousand. The gain is the premises, twenty-seven thousand. The profit is rupees twelve thousand, shared three to two to one: Anshuman rupees six thousand, Bhairavi rupees four thousand and Chiranjeev rupees two thousand.

slides.heading: Reserves and accumulated profits or losses

rows: General reserve, credit balance of profit and loss
Credited to **all** partners' capitals, old ratio
Debit balance of profit and loss, advertisement suspense
Debited to **all** partners' capitals, old ratio
Claim first; balance credited; excess claim a revaluation loss
Fall in investments first; balance credited; excess fall a revaluation loss

visual.alt: Table of reserves on retirement or death: reserves and credit balances are credited, and accumulated losses and deferred revenue expenditure debited, to all the partners in the old ratio; special reserves first meet the claim or the fall

slides.narration: Reserves and undistributed profits were earned while the outgoing partner was a member, so they are credited to all the partners in the old ratio. Accumulated losses and advertisement suspense are debited the same way. A workmen compensation reserve first meets the claim, and an investment fluctuation reserve first meets the fall in investments; only the balance is shared.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: reserves of Gulmohar Marble Polishers
slides.body_md: General reserve ₹36,000; workmen compensation reserve ₹15,000 against a claim of ₹9,000; advertisement suspense ₹12,000.

rows: *(Being general reserve credited to all the partners in 3 : 2 : 1)*
*(Being claim provided and the balance of the reserve credited in 3 : 2 : 1)*

visual.alt: Journal of worked example six: general reserve 36,000 credited three to two to one; workmen compensation reserve 15,000 meets the claim of 9,000 and the balance 6,000 is credited; advertisement suspense 12,000 debited three to two to one

slides.narration: The general reserve of rupees thirty-six thousand is credited three to two to one. The workmen compensation reserve first provides for the claim of rupees nine thousand, and the balance of rupees six thousand is credited. The advertisement suspense of rupees twelve thousand is a past loss, so it is debited to all three partners.

slides.heading: Quick check: deferred revenue expenditure
slides.body_md: Who bears a past loss carried on the assets side?
slides.narration: Ask when the expense was incurred, and who was a partner then.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: New share − old share; a negative result is a sacrifice
Continuing partners keep their old ratio
Gaining partners Dr. (gaining ratio), outgoing partner Cr. (his share × goodwill)
Settlement − his adjusted capital = his share
Written off among all partners, old ratio

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: gain is new minus old share; with nothing agreed the old ratio continues; the gaining partners pay the outgoing partner for goodwill; hidden goodwill is the excess of the settlement over his capital; book goodwill, revaluation, reserves and losses go to all partners in the old ratio

slides.narration: To sum up: gain is new share minus old share, and with nothing agreed the old ratio continues. The gaining partners pay the outgoing partner his share of goodwill, and a partner who sacrifices is paid too. Hidden goodwill is the excess of the settlement over his adjusted capital. Book goodwill, revaluation, reserves and losses all go to every partner in the old ratio.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Always **show the gaining ratio**; with a stated new ratio it is rarely the old ratio.
Check every continuing partner: one may **sacrifice** and must then be credited for goodwill.
Share revaluation, reserves and losses among **all** partners, the outgoing one included.
Never open a goodwill account; write off any **book goodwill** first.
Write a **narration** under every journal entry.
slides.narration: A few habits save marks. Always show the gaining ratio, because a stated new ratio rarely gives the old ratio. Check every continuing partner, since one may sacrifice. Share revaluation, reserves and losses among all the partners, the outgoing one included. Never open a goodwill account, and write off any goodwill already in the books first.

nodes.label: Amount due and capital accounts
Balance Sheet (horizontal)
Loan account
Adjusting capitals
Death: profit till death
Executor's account

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the amount due and capital accounts, the new balance sheet in horizontal form, the loan account, adjusting capitals, profit till death, and the executor's account
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In the first part we settled ratios, goodwill, revaluation and reserves. Now we bring them together. We find the amount due to the outgoing partner, decide how it is paid, keep his loan account, adjust the continuing partners' capitals, deal with the special points on death, and draw up the new balance sheet.

slides.heading: The amount due to an outgoing partner

rows: Share of reserves and undistributed profit
Share of accumulated losses, advertisement suspense, book goodwill
Share of goodwill (from the gaining partners)
Interest on capital; on death, profit till death

visual.alt: Table of what makes up the amount due to an outgoing partner: credits for capital, revaluation profit, reserves, his share of goodwill, interest on capital and, on death, profit till death; debits for losses, drawings and interest on drawings

slides.narration: The amount due is simply the closing balance of his capital account. It starts with his capital and any current account balance. Add his share of revaluation profit, reserves and goodwill, and on death his share of profit and interest on capital to that date. Deduct his share of losses, his drawings and interest on them. What remains is what the firm owes him.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: capital accounts of Gulmohar Marble Polishers
slides.body_md: Bhairavi's due is paid ₹34,000 by cheque; the balance becomes her **loan**.

visual.alt: Partners' capital accounts of Gulmohar Marble Polishers: all three credited with revaluation profit and reserves and debited with advertisement suspense; Anshuman and Chiranjeev debited 30,000 and 10,000 for goodwill; Bhairavi's 1,74,000 settled by bank 34,000 and loan 1,40,000 rupees

slides.narration: All three partners take their shares of the revaluation profit and the reserves, and bear the advertisement suspense. Anshuman and Chiranjeev are then debited rupees thirty thousand and rupees ten thousand for goodwill, credited to Bhairavi. Her account closes at rupees one lakh seventy-four thousand: rupees thirty-four thousand by cheque and rupees one lakh forty thousand to her loan account.

slides.heading: Worked example 7 (continued): the new Balance Sheet
slides.body_md: Horizontal form; reserves gone; the claim, the rent bill and Bhairavi's loan appear as liabilities.

visual.alt: Balance sheet of Gulmohar Marble Polishers after Bhairavi's retirement, totalling 4,65,000 rupees: creditors, the workmen compensation claim, outstanding rent, Bhairavi's loan and two capitals; bank 6,000, debtors net of provision and assets at revised values
visual.caption: Horizontal form: reserves gone, loan in, revised values.

slides.narration: The new balance sheet shows creditors, the compensation claim, the rent bill and Bhairavi's loan of rupees one lakh forty thousand, followed by two capitals. On the other side the bank has fallen to rupees six thousand, debtors are shown net of the provision, and the premises and machinery appear at revised values. Both sides total rupees four lakh sixty-five thousand.

slides.heading: How the amount due is settled
slides.body_md: If nothing is agreed and the money stays in the business, **Section 37** applies.

headers: How the amount due is settled
rows: Outgoing partner's Capital A/c Dr. To Bank A/c
Left with the firm as a loan
Outgoing partner's Capital A/c Dr. To his Loan A/c
Interest A/c Dr. To Loan A/c; Loan A/c Dr. To Bank A/c
Section 37: share of profit from his share of property, or 6% per annum interest, at his option

visual.alt: Table of the modes of settling the amount due: paid at once through the bank, transferred to a loan, partly each, instalments with interest, and the Section thirty-seven option of a share of profits or interest at six per cent when nothing is agreed

slides.narration: The amount due may be paid at once, left with the firm as a loan, or partly each. A loan is usually repaid in instalments with interest on the balance. If the money stays in the business and nothing is agreed, Section thirty-seven lets the outgoing partner choose between a share of the profits earned with his share of the property and interest at six per cent a year.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: Bhairavi's loan account
slides.body_md: Her loan of ₹1,40,000 is repaid in four equal yearly instalments from 31 March 2027, each with interest at 10% on the balance.

visual.alt: Bhairavi's loan account over four years: 1,40,000 rupees credited on retirement; each year interest at ten per cent on the balance is credited and an instalment of 35,000 plus that interest is paid, so payments fall from 49,000 to 38,500

slides.narration: Each instalment of principal is rupees thirty-five thousand. In the first year interest is ten per cent of rupees one lakh forty thousand, that is rupees fourteen thousand, so she receives rupees forty-nine thousand. As the balance falls, so does the interest, and the last payment is rupees thirty-eight thousand five hundred. Every year the account balances, and after four years it closes.

slides.heading: Worked example 9: interest accrued but not due
slides.body_md: Shefali Makhana Traders, Sitamarhi (imagined): Prasoon retires on 30 September 2026; ₹90,000 is repaid in three yearly instalments each 30 September, with 10% interest. Books close on 31 March.

visual.alt: Prasoon's loan account: 90,000 rupees from thirtieth September; on each thirty-first March six months' interest is credited although not yet due; each thirtieth September an instalment of 30,000 is paid with a full year's interest; payments 39,000, 36,000, 33,000

slides.narration: On thirty-first March the loan has run for six months, so rupees four thousand five hundred of interest is credited even though it is not yet due. On thirtieth September the next six months' interest is credited and an instalment of rupees thirty thousand is paid with a full year's interest, rupees thirty-nine thousand in all. The pattern repeats until the loan is cleared.

slides.body_md: Think about what the firm now owes.

slides.heading: Adjusting the continuing partners' capitals
bullets: **Total capital** is agreed, or equals their adjusted capitals **plus** the cash needed to pay the outgoing partner and keep a minimum bank balance.
**Required capital** = total × new share; the difference is brought in or withdrawn.

nodes.label: Total capital of the new firm (agreed, or capitals + cash needed)

sections.heading: 1. Retirement and death of a partner
sections.body_md:
A partner who leaves **reconstitutes** the firm: the old agreement ends, the remaining partners carry on, and the books are adjusted rather than closed.

- **Retirement (Section 32, Indian Partnership Act, 1932):** with the consent of all the other partners, under an express agreement, or by written notice in a partnership at will. A retired partner remains liable to third parties for acts of the firm until public notice of his retirement is given.
- **Death:** subject to the deed, death dissolves the firm (Section 42); most deeds therefore provide that the surviving partners continue.
- The outgoing partner (or his executor) is entitled to his capital and his share of everything the firm earned or built up while he was a partner.

**Matters settled:** new and gaining ratios; goodwill; revaluation; reserves and accumulated profits or losses; profit till death (on death); amount due and its payment; capitals and the new Balance Sheet.

*Not in the ISC 2027 syllabus for this chapter:* memorandum revaluation account, and joint life and individual life policies.

The legal representative who receives a deceased partner's dues on behalf of his estate.

sections.heading: 3. Goodwill, book goodwill and hidden goodwill
sections.body_md:

**Amount due** = closing balance of the outgoing partner's capital account (see the table).

**Settlement:** paid by bank; transferred to his **Loan A/c**; or both. If unpaid with no agreement, **Section 37** gives him, at his option, the share of profits attributable to the use of his share of the property, or interest at **6% per annum** on it.

**Loan account (instalments with interest):** interest on the balance outstanding is credited to the loan account (Interest A/c Dr. To Loan A/c); each instalment plus interest is paid (Loan A/c Dr. To Bank A/c). Interest for months already run at the year end is credited even when payable later — **interest accrued but not due** — and is carried down in the balance; interest credited on the instalment date is **accrued and due**.

**Death:** the balance of the deceased partner's capital account is transferred to his **Executor's A/c**, which is paid by bank and/or transferred to the **Executor's Loan A/c**.

sections.heading: 8. Balance Sheet after retirement or death (horizontal form)
sections.body_md:
Prepared in **horizontal form**, liabilities and capitals on the left, assets on the right.

- **Liabilities:** creditors and other outside liabilities, any claim or outstanding expense brought in, the **retiring partner's loan** or **executor's loan**, and the continuing partners' closing capitals.
- **Assets:** revised values (debtors less provision), the **bank** after payments and any cash brought in, and **Profit and Loss Suspense** if used on death.
- **Gone:** reserves, accumulated losses, advertisement suspense and book goodwill.

**Check:** both sides total; if not, recompute the bank.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Assuming the gaining ratio is the old ratio when a new ratio is stated.
- Forgetting a continuing partner who **sacrifices** and must be credited for goodwill.
- Sharing revaluation, reserves or losses only among the continuing partners; the outgoing partner shares them too.
- Opening a goodwill account, or leaving book goodwill in the balance sheet.
- Ignoring interest **accrued but not due** at the year end in a loan account.
- Counting the months to death wrongly, or using the wrong basis for profit till death.
- Showing Profit and Loss Suspense or the executor's loan on the wrong side; drawing the Balance Sheet in vertical form.

**How marks are usually awarded (SOYL chapter tests on the ISC default pattern)**
- 1 mark: objective items.
- 2 marks: a ratio calculation, hidden goodwill, profit till death with its entry, or a capital adjustment.
- 3 marks: a Revaluation Account, a set of reserve entries, a loan account, or capital and executor's accounts.
- 5 marks in parts, e.g. (a) 2 + (b) 3: ratios and goodwill with a Revaluation Account, or the amount due with a loan account.
- Full practical (practice, 8 marks): Revaluation Account about 2, capital accounts about 3, Balance Sheet about 3; working notes earn step marks.

**Figures in SOYL practice** are imagined; your board paper will give its own.

questions.stem_md: Kumudini wants to leave Palash Salt Pans, an imagined firm at Ponneri. The deed says nothing about retirement and the firm is not a partnership at will. Under Section 32 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, she may retire

options.text_md: by giving notice only to the partner with the largest capital
with the consent of all the other partners
only after the firm itself has been dissolved
by filing a notice with the Registrar of Firms, without asking her partners

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** with the consent of all the other partners. Section 32 permits retirement with the consent of all the other partners, under an express agreement among them, or by written notice when the partnership is at will; only the first route is open to her.

questions.stem_md: The deed of Swarna Bell-Metal Works, an imagined firm at Paithan, is silent on what happens if a partner dies. Under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, the death of one of its partners

options.text_md: makes the deceased partner's heir a partner automatically, with the same share
converts the firm into a sole proprietorship of the eldest surviving partner
has no legal effect until the Registrar of Firms approves a new deed
dissolves the firm, which is why most deeds provide that the surviving partners will carry on the business

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** dissolves the firm, which is why most deeds provide that the surviving partners will carry on the business. Subject to a contract among the partners, a firm is dissolved by the death of a partner. Deeds therefore usually let the survivors continue, and the books are then reconstituted rather than closed.

questions.stem_md: Ilavarasi, Janardan and Kshama share the profits of Amaltas Brass Lamps, an imagined firm at Tiruchirappalli, 4 : 3 : 2. Kshama retires and the partners agree on nothing about future shares. The new profit-sharing ratio of Ilavarasi and Janardan is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 4 : 3. When nothing is agreed, the continuing partners keep their old ratio: Ilavarasi 4/7 and Janardan 3/7, so their gaining ratio is also 4 : 3.

questions.stem_md: In Harsingar Banana Fibre Works, an imagined firm at Pollachi, Lakshana, Murugan and Nitya share profits 5 : 3 : 2. Nitya retires; Lakshana acquires 1/10 of the firm's profit from her and Murugan acquires the other 1/10. The new ratio of Lakshana and Murugan is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 3 : 2. Add each acquisition to the old share: Lakshana 5/10 + 1/10 = 3/5 and Murugan 3/10 + 1/10 = 2/5.

questions.stem_md: Orpita, Pranit and Sukhada run Rajnigandha Brassware, an imagined firm at Pandharpur, sharing profits 3 : 2 : 1. When Pranit retires, Orpita and Sukhada agree to share future profits 5 : 3. Their gaining ratio is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 3 : 5. Gain = new share − old share: Orpita 5/8 − 1/2 = 1/8 = 3/24 and Sukhada 3/8 − 1/6 = 5/24, so the gaining ratio is 3 : 5, not the new ratio.

questions.stem_md: Tanushree, Udayan and Vaibhavi share the profits of Chameli Ghee Dairy, an imagined firm at Gokak, 2 : 2 : 1. On Vaibhavi's retirement, Tanushree and Udayan agree to share 1 : 3 in future. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹1,20,000. The adjustment entry for goodwill is

options.text_md: Udayan's Capital A/c Dr. ₹42,000 To Vaibhavi's Capital A/c ₹24,000 and To Tanushree's Capital A/c ₹18,000
Tanushree's and Udayan's Capital A/cs Dr. ₹12,000 each To Vaibhavi's Capital A/c ₹24,000
Udayan's Capital A/c Dr. ₹24,000 To Vaibhavi's Capital A/c ₹24,000
Goodwill A/c Dr. ₹1,20,000 To all three partners' Capital A/cs in 2 : 2 : 1

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Udayan's Capital A/c Dr. ₹42,000 To Vaibhavi's Capital A/c ₹24,000 and To Tanushree's Capital A/c ₹18,000. Tanushree falls from 2/5 to 1/4, a sacrifice of 3/20, while Udayan rises from 2/5 to 3/4, a gain of 7/20. Udayan alone pays: 7/20 of 1,20,000 = 42,000, of which Vaibhavi gets 1/5 of the goodwill (24,000) and Tanushree 3/20 (18,000).

questions.stem_md: When a partner leaves Shukti Pearl Traders, an imagined firm at Thoothukudi, its accountant computes each continuing partner's gain. That gain is

options.text_md: the continuing partner's old share minus his new share
the outgoing partner's share divided equally among the continuing partners
the continuing partner's new share divided by his old share
the continuing partner's new share minus his old share

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the continuing partner's new share minus his old share. A continuing partner gains when his share rises, so the gain is measured as new share less old share; the ratio of these gains is the gaining ratio.

questions.stem_md: True or false? If the deed of Neelkurinji Bamboo Craft, an imagined firm at Hojai, is silent about future shares when one partner retires, the continuing partners gain in the same proportion as their old profit-sharing ratio.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** With no agreement they carry on in their old ratio, so each one's gain is his old share scaled up, and the gains stand in that same old ratio.

questions.stem_md: When Wazir retires from Kasturi Desert Safaris, an imagined firm at Jaisalmer, the partners who stay on compensate him for goodwill in the proportion of their extra shares, called the ___ ratio.
questions.solution_md: It is the gaining ratio, worked out as each continuing partner's new share minus his old share.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** On the retirement of a partner from Bakul Ceramics, an imagined pottery firm, the retiring partner's share of goodwill is debited to the continuing partners in their gaining ratio.

**Reason (R):** On the admission of a new partner, the sacrificing ratio is the ratio in which the old partners give up their shares in his favour.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is a correct statement of the retirement entry and R correctly defines the sacrificing ratio, but R is about admission and does not explain why the gaining ratio is used on retirement.

questions.stem_md: Yashodhara, Zoravar and Abhilasha share the profits of Saptaparni Eucalyptus Oil Distillers, an imagined firm at Coonoor, 3 : 3 : 2. Abhilasha retires, and her share is taken over by Yashodhara and Zoravar in the ratio 3 : 1. Calculate the new profit-sharing ratio and the gaining ratio.
questions.solution_md: Split the outgoing share in the agreed proportion and add each part to the old share; the gains are those parts, so their ratio is the agreed one.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Abhilasha's 1/4 is taken in 3 : 1: Yashodhara 3/8 + 1/4 × 3/4 = 9/16; Zoravar 3/8 + 1/4 × 1/4 = 7/16; new ratio = **9 : 7**.
2. Gain = new share − old share: Yashodhara 9/16 − 3/8 = 3/16 (gain); Zoravar 7/16 − 3/8 = 1/16 (gain). Gaining ratio = **3 : 1**.

questions.stem_md: The partners of Kanchanar Stone Crushers, an imagined firm at Barmer, admitted a partner three years ago and now one of them is retiring. State two differences between the sacrificing ratio they used then and the gaining ratio they must use now.
questions.solution_md: Contrast the two on when each arises and how it is measured (or what it is used for); any two bases earn the marks.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Basis | Sacrificing ratio | Gaining ratio |
|---|---|---|
| When it is computed | On admission of a partner (or a change in ratio) | On retirement or death of a partner (or a change in ratio) |
| Formula | Old share − new share | New share − old share |
| Use | Shares the incoming partner's premium for goodwill among the partners who give up profit | Charges the outgoing partner's share of goodwill to the partners who acquire it |

marking_scheme.step: First difference (for example, when it is computed)

questions.stem_md: Bhanumati, Chakrapani and Dhriti share the profits of Jacaranda Tea Chests, an imagined firm at Pasighat, 4 : 3 : 2. Dhriti retires and Bhanumati and Chakrapani agree to share future profits 1 : 2. Goodwill is valued at ₹90,000. Show the gain or sacrifice of each continuing partner and pass the journal entry for goodwill.
questions.solution_md: Compare old and new shares for every continuing partner; one who loses under the new ratio is credited with the outgoing partner.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. New ratio (Bhanumati : Chakrapani) as agreed = **1 : 2**.
2. Gain = new share − old share: Bhanumati 1/3 − 4/9 = −1/9 (sacrifice); Chakrapani 2/3 − 1/3 = 1/3 (gain). Gaining ratio = **only Chakrapani gains**.
3. Bhanumati gives up 1/9 even though a partner is leaving, so she is compensated along with Dhriti: Dhriti 90,000 × 2/9 = ₹20,000, Bhanumati 90,000 × 1/9 = ₹10,000; Chakrapani pays 90,000 × 1/3 = ₹30,000.

questions.stem_md: Elango, Farida and Govardhan share the profits of Semal Kinnow Growers, an imagined orchard firm at Ropar, 5 : 4 : 3. On Govardhan's retirement Elango takes 1/12 of the firm's profit from him and Farida takes the remaining 2/12. Goodwill is valued at ₹96,000. With how much is Farida's capital account debited for goodwill (in ₹)?
questions.solution_md: Farida's gain is the 2/12 she acquires, so she is debited 96,000 × 2/12 = 16,000, that is ₹16,000; Elango is debited 8,000.

questions.stem_md: Haider retires from Tendu Cycle Works, an imagined firm at Pimpri, and no goodwill account is opened. His share of the firm's goodwill is recorded by debiting

options.text_md: Haider's capital account and crediting the gaining partners' capital accounts
the gaining partners' capital accounts and crediting Haider's capital account
a goodwill account and crediting all the partners' capital accounts in the old ratio
Haider's capital account and crediting a goodwill account

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the gaining partners' capital accounts and crediting Haider's capital account. Accounting Standard 26 does not allow self-generated goodwill to be raised, so the partners who acquire Haider's share pay him through their capital accounts.

questions.stem_md: Jitendra, Kiranmala and Lalitendu share the profits of Sheesham Rafting, an imagined adventure firm at Pachmarhi, 2 : 2 : 1. Kiranmala retires. Goodwill is valued at three years' purchase of the average profit of ₹40,000. Kiranmala's capital account is credited for goodwill with
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹48,000. Goodwill = 40,000 × 3 = 1,20,000; her share = 1,20,000 × 2/5 = 48,000, debited to Jitendra and Lalitendu in 2 : 1.

questions.stem_md: The balance sheet of Arjuna Cotton Ginners, an imagined firm at Wani, shows goodwill of ₹30,000 when Omvati, one of its three partners, retires. Madhukar, Nirupama and Omvati share profits 3 : 2 : 1. The book goodwill is written off by debiting

options.text_md: only Madhukar's and Nirupama's capital accounts, in 3 : 2
all three partners' capital accounts with ₹15,000, ₹10,000 and ₹5,000
Omvati's capital account with the whole ₹30,000
the continuing partners' capital accounts in their gaining ratio

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** all three partners' capital accounts with ₹15,000, ₹10,000 and ₹5,000. Goodwill already in the books belongs to the firm before the retirement, so every partner, Omvati included, bears it in the old ratio: 30,000 × 3/6, 2/6 and 1/6.

questions.stem_md: Purnima holds a 1/4 share in Kachnar Spice Haulers, an imagined firm at Ranni. When she retires, her capital after all adjustments other than goodwill stands at ₹1,15,000, and the other partners agree to pay her ₹1,40,000 in full settlement. The goodwill of the firm implied by this settlement is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹1,00,000. Her share of hidden goodwill = 1,40,000 − 1,15,000 = 25,000; the firm's goodwill = 25,000 ÷ 1/4 = 1,00,000.

questions.stem_md: Ranjana, Shrikant and Tithi share the profits of Kaner Roof Tiles, an imagined firm at Ichalkaranji, 4 : 3 : 2. On Tithi's retirement the Revaluation Account shows a loss of ₹18,000. Tithi's capital account is debited with

options.text_md: nothing, because only the continuing partners bear the loss

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹4,000. The loss arose while all three were partners, so it is shared 4 : 3 : 2 and Tithi bears 18,000 × 2/9 = 4,000.

questions.stem_md: When a partner retires from Akshay Fisheries, an imagined firm at Chhatrapur, its Workmen Compensation Reserve stands at ₹20,000 but the claim now admitted is ₹26,000. The correct treatment is that

options.text_md: the reserve of ₹20,000 is credited to all the partners and the claim is charged to the retiring partner alone
₹6,000 is credited to all the partners' capital accounts in the old ratio
the claim is ignored, because a reserve already exists for it
the whole reserve goes towards the claim and the excess ₹6,000 is debited to the Revaluation Account

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the whole reserve goes towards the claim and the excess ₹6,000 is debited to the Revaluation Account. The reserve is used up against the liability; the shortfall is a loss of the firm before the retirement, so it passes through the Revaluation Account to all the partners.

questions.stem_md: Sugandh Rubber Traders, an imagined firm at Pathanamthitta, carries an Investment Fluctuation Reserve of ₹12,000 against investments of ₹80,000, whose market value on a partner's retirement is ₹74,000. After meeting the fall, the reserve leaves

options.text_md: ₹12,000 to be credited to all the partners, the fall being ignored
₹6,000 to be debited to the Revaluation Account
₹6,000 to be credited to all the partners' capital accounts in the old ratio
₹6,000 to be credited only to the continuing partners

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹6,000 to be credited to all the partners' capital accounts in the old ratio. The fall of 6,000 is met from the reserve; the balance 12,000 − 6,000 = 6,000 is an accumulated profit of all the partners.

questions.stem_md: At the time a partner retires from Swarnim Packaging, an imagined firm at Badlapur, its balance sheet shows an advertisement suspense account on the assets side. This balance is

options.text_md: debited to the continuing partners' capital accounts in their gaining ratio
debited to all the partners' capital accounts, the retiring partner included, in the old ratio
carried forward unchanged in the balance sheet of the new firm
credited to the Revaluation Account

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** debited to all the partners' capital accounts, the retiring partner included, in the old ratio. Deferred revenue expenditure is a past loss of the old firm, so it is written off against every partner in the old ratio before the retiring partner is settled.

questions.stem_md: Before settling with a retiring partner, the partners of Ratnakar Fish Meal, an imagined firm at Malvan, revalue the firm's assets and liabilities. The main purpose is

options.text_md: to give the retiring partner his share of the gains or losses in value that arose while he was a partner
to raise a goodwill account in the books at its full value
to reduce the income tax payable by the continuing partners
to fix the new profit-sharing ratio of the continuing partners

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** to give the retiring partner his share of the gains or losses in value that arose while he was a partner. Book values may be out of date; revaluing them makes sure the outgoing partner neither gains nor loses from changes in value up to the date he leaves.

questions.stem_md: True or false? When Vasanti retires from Nakshatra Cashew Exporters, an imagined firm at Ponda, the profit on revaluation is shared by all the partners, Vasanti included, in their old ratio.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The rise in values took place while she was a partner, so she takes her old share of the profit before her account is settled.

questions.stem_md: True or false? If the continuing partners of Dhruva Silk Reelers, an imagined firm, agree to pay a retiring partner more than the balance of his capital account after all adjustments, the excess is credited to the continuing partners' capital accounts.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The excess is the retiring partner's share of hidden goodwill: it is credited to him and debited to the gaining partners in their gaining ratio.

questions.stem_md: Yeshwant, who has a 1/5 share in Shukra Jaggery Mill, an imagined firm at Ichalkaranji, retires. His capital after revaluation and reserves is ₹86,000, and his partners settle with him for ₹1,02,000. What is the goodwill of the firm implied by this settlement (in ₹)?
questions.solution_md: His share of goodwill = 1,02,000 − 86,000 = 16,000; firm's goodwill = 16,000 ÷ 1/5 = 80,000, that is ₹80,000.

questions.stem_md: Abhijit, Bratati and Zubeida are equal partners in Ashwini Jute Twine, an imagined firm at Serampore. On Zubeida's retirement the building is raised by ₹30,000, stock is reduced by ₹9,000 and a provision of ₹3,000 is made for doubtful debts. How much revaluation profit is credited to Zubeida (in ₹)?
questions.solution_md: Revaluation profit = 30,000 − 9,000 − 3,000 = 18,000; Zubeida's one-third = 6,000, that is ₹6,000.

questions.stem_md: On Sumitra's retirement from Revati Coal Briquettes, an imagined firm, a fall in the value of machinery is ___ to the Revaluation Account, and the resulting profit or loss is shared by ___ the partners in their old ratio.
questions.solution_md: A fall in an asset is a loss, so it is debited; the result belongs to all the partners, Sumitra included, in the old ratio.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When Eshwari retires from Anuradha Hill Lodges, an imagined resort firm, the general reserve in its books is credited to all the partners' capital accounts, Eshwari's included, in their old ratio.

questions.stem_md: A junior accountant at Tamra Copperware, an imagined firm at Tirupati, asks why three steps are taken when a partner retires. Explain briefly why (a) the assets and liabilities are revalued, (b) the general reserve is shared among all the partners, and (c) the continuing partners compensate the retiring partner for goodwill.
questions.solution_md: Each step protects the retiring partner's right to what the firm earned or built up while he was a partner.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Book values may differ from current values. The gain or loss in value arose while the retiring partner was a member, so revaluation gives him his share and keeps the continuing partners from bearing or enjoying it later.

**(b)** The reserve consists of profits kept back in earlier years while all the partners, including the retiring one, shared profits; it is therefore their common property in the old ratio.

**(c)** The firm's reputation, built partly by the retiring partner, will earn future profits for the continuing partners alone. Those who gain his share pay for it in their gaining ratio; no goodwill account is raised under Accounting Standard 26.

Their capitals are ₹1,40,000, ₹1,20,000 and ₹70,000, and a general reserve of ₹25,000 stands in the books. Omisha retires on 31 March 2026; Malati and Neelkanth will share 3 : 2. Land is revalued upwards by ₹10,000 and goodwill is valued at ₹1,50,000. Omisha is paid in full by cheque, and the total capital of the new firm is fixed at ₹2,50,000 in the new ratio, surpluses and shortfalls being settled in cash.

(a) Show the gain of each continuing partner and pass the entry for goodwill. [2]

(b) Prepare the Partners' Capital Accounts. [3]
questions.solution_md: A partner whose share is the same before and after pays nothing for goodwill; capital adjustment comes only after the retiring partner is settled.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)**
1. New ratio (Malati : Neelkanth) as agreed = **3 : 2**.
2. Gain = new share − old share: Malati 3/5 − 2/5 = 1/5 (gain); Neelkanth 2/5 − 2/5 = 0 (no change). Gaining ratio = **only Malati gains**.
3. Neelkanth's share does not change, so Malati alone pays for Omisha's 1/5 of goodwill: 1,50,000 × 1/5 = ₹30,000.

| Particulars | Dr (₹) | Cr (₹) |
| --- | --: | --: |
| Malati's Capital A/c Dr. | 30,000 |  |
| To Omisha's Capital A/c |  | 30,000 |
| *(Being Omisha's share of goodwill charged to Malati, the only gaining partner)* |  |  |

**(b) Working notes** (ratios as in (a))
1. Revaluation: profit ₹10,000, shared by all the partners in the old ratio 2 : 2 : 1 (Malati ₹4,000, Neelkanth ₹4,000, Omisha ₹2,000).
2. General Reserve ₹25,000 is credited to all the partners in the old ratio 2 : 2 : 1 (Malati ₹10,000, Neelkanth ₹10,000, Omisha ₹5,000).
3. Goodwill ₹1,50,000: Omisha's share = 1,50,000 × 1/5 = ₹30,000. Debited to the gaining partner (Malati ₹30,000); credited Omisha ₹30,000.
4. Amount due to Omisha = ₹1,07,000: paid in full by bank.
5. Total capital of the new firm (agreed) = **₹2,50,000**.
6. Malati: required 2,50,000 × 3/5 = ₹1,50,000; capital after adjustments ₹1,24,000; brings in ₹26,000.
7. Neelkanth: required 2,50,000 × 2/5 = ₹1,00,000; capital after adjustments ₹1,34,000; withdraws ₹34,000.
8. Bank: ₹1,20,000 (opening) − ₹1,07,000 (paid to Omisha) + ₹26,000 (Malati brings in) − ₹34,000 (Neelkanth withdraws) = ₹5,000.

**Partners' Capital Accounts**

| To Omisha's Capital A/c | 30,000 |  |  | By Balance b/d | 1,40,000 | 1,20,000 | 70,000 |
| To Bank A/c |  | 34,000 | 1,07,000 | By Revaluation A/c (profit) | 4,000 | 4,000 | 2,000 |
|  |  |  |  | By General Reserve A/c | 10,000 | 10,000 | 5,000 |
|  |  |  |  | By Malati's Capital A/c |  |  | 30,000 |
| To Balance c/d | 1,50,000 | 1,00,000 |  | By Bank A/c | 26,000 |  |  |
| **Total** | **1,80,000** | **1,34,000** | **1,07,000** | **Total** | **1,80,000** | **1,34,000** | **1,07,000** |

nowhere, because loans of partners are kept off the balance sheet

questions.stem_md:
Vishwas, Yojana and Akshita are partners in Firoza Blue Pottery, an imagined firm at Sanganer, sharing profits 3 : 2 : 1. Their Balance Sheet as at 31 March 2026 was:

| Liabilities | ₹ | Assets | ₹ |
| --- | --: | --- | --: |
| Creditors | 40,000 | Bank | 22,000 |
| General Reserve | 12,000 | Debtors | 48,000 |
| Profit and Loss A/c | 18,000 | Stock | 55,000 |
| Vishwas's Capital | 1,40,000 | Furniture | 25,000 |
| Yojana's Capital | 90,000 | Plant | 1,00,000 |
| Akshita's Capital | 50,000 | Land | 1,00,000 |
| **Total** | **3,50,000** | **Total** | **3,50,000** |

Yojana retires on that date; Vishwas and Akshita continue in their old ratio. (a) Land is appreciated by 18% and plant depreciated by 6%. (b) Yojana is to be paid ₹1,28,000 in full settlement, at once; nothing else is said about goodwill. (c) Vishwas and Akshita bring in just enough cash to pay Yojana and leave ₹20,000 in the bank, so that their capitals are in their profit-sharing ratio.

Prepare the Revaluation Account, the Partners' Capital Accounts and the Balance Sheet of the reconstituted firm in horizontal form.
questions.solution_md: Settle everything except goodwill first; the excess of the settlement over Yojana's capital then reveals goodwill, and only after that can the cash to be brought in be worked out.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Working notes**

1. Nothing is agreed, so Vishwas and Akshita continue in their old ratio: new ratio = **3 : 1**.
2. Gain = new share − old share: Vishwas 3/4 − 1/2 = 1/4 (gain); Akshita 1/4 − 1/6 = 1/12 (gain). Gaining ratio = **3 : 1**.
3. Revaluation: gains ₹18,000 − losses ₹6,000 = profit ₹12,000, shared by all the partners in the old ratio 3 : 2 : 1 (Vishwas ₹6,000, Yojana ₹4,000, Akshita ₹2,000).
4. General Reserve ₹12,000 is credited to all the partners in the old ratio 3 : 2 : 1 (Vishwas ₹6,000, Yojana ₹4,000, Akshita ₹2,000).
5. Profit and Loss ₹18,000 is credited to all the partners in the old ratio 3 : 2 : 1 (Vishwas ₹9,000, Yojana ₹6,000, Akshita ₹3,000).
6. Hidden goodwill: Yojana is to receive ₹1,28,000 in full settlement against a capital of ₹1,04,000 after all other adjustments; the excess ₹24,000 is Yojana's share of goodwill. Firm's goodwill = ₹24,000 ÷ 1/3 = **₹72,000**.
7. Goodwill ₹72,000: Yojana's share = 72,000 × 1/3 = ₹24,000. Debited to the gaining partners in 3 : 1 (Vishwas ₹18,000, Akshita ₹6,000); credited Yojana ₹24,000.
8. Amount due to Yojana = ₹1,28,000: paid in full by bank.
9. Cash needed = ₹1,28,000 (payment) + ₹20,000 (minimum balance) − ₹22,000 (bank) = ₹1,26,000. Total capital of the new firm = ₹1,43,000 + ₹51,000 + ₹1,26,000 = **₹3,20,000**.
10. Vishwas: required 3,20,000 × 3/4 = ₹2,40,000; capital after adjustments ₹1,43,000; brings in ₹97,000.
11. Akshita: required 3,20,000 × 1/4 = ₹80,000; capital after adjustments ₹51,000; brings in ₹29,000.
12. Bank: ₹22,000 (opening) − ₹1,28,000 (paid to Yojana) + ₹97,000 (Vishwas brings in) + ₹29,000 (Akshita brings in) = ₹20,000.
